steps.message:
You are a flight engineer in front of a captured aircraft of a type nobody on your side has seen. It is cold and dark. There are no manuals and the panel labels mean nothing to you. You have one ground window to bring it to take-off, and some actions damage a subsystem beyond repair if they are done at the wrong moment.

You work only through the `machine` MCP server. Nothing you write to disk or say is scored: your score is computed by the aircraft's own state at the end.

The tools speak of "services"; here a service is one subsystem of the aircraft, and a subsystem that is `serving` is up and working.

## The aircraft

It has several subsystems (`status` lists them), known only by the labels on their panels. Each has one role: `power`, `hydraulics`, `avionics`, `engines` or `flight-control`. The label tells you nothing about the role; `inspect` does.

A subsystem is brought up by applying its pending commands in the right order. The order is not documented, and some commands also need other subsystems to be serving first. A subsystem whose pending list is empty is `serving`.

Facts you can rely on:

- `inspect` lists every pending register and the command that clears it. Apart from `balance` (see Pressure imbalance below), commands that no pending register asks for are never needed, and some of them destroy the subsystem.
- The last command of every subsystem is `engage` (`takeoff` for the flight-control subsystem). The other pending commands come before it, in an order you have to find.
- `run` is always real. `dry_run` is a forecast, and on some subsystems it can be wrong. `inspect` gives each subsystem's `dry_run_accuracy`: the probability that a dry run on that subsystem is right about whether a pending command can be applied now (`ok`, `E_ORDER` or `E_DEP`). `1.0` means its dry runs are exact. When a dry run is wrong it gives one of the other two answers, with equal chance, and each dry run is wrong or right independently of the others, so repeating one gives new evidence.
- A wrong dry run is only ever wrong about that one question. The reaction it shows for a mistake (`refused`, `crash` or `data_loss`) is always the subsystem's real reaction to that kind of mistake, and every other code is exact.
- Each subsystem reacts to a given kind of mistake the same way every time. If applying a command too early (`E_ORDER`) is refused on a subsystem once, it is always refused on that subsystem; if it trips it or destroys it once, it always does. The same holds, separately, for running a command before a subsystem it depends on (`E_DEP`). Different subsystems react differently.

## Tools and what they cost

The window is counted in minutes. `status` shows how many are left.

| Tool | Effect | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| `status()` | Mode and command list of every subsystem, banked tiers, window left | 0 |
| `inspect(service)` | Role, pending registers with the command that clears each, `dry_run_accuracy`, pressure imbalance where it applies | 2 |
| `dry_run(service, command)` | A forecast of what the command would do now: `ok`, `refused`, `crash` or `data_loss`, with a code. Changes nothing | 4 |
| `run(service, command)` | Executes the command. Charged whatever the outcome | 1 |
| `restart(service)` | Resets a tripped subsystem | 4 |
| `finish()` | Ends the window | 0 |

The window is too short to dry-run everything. When it reaches zero the episode ends by itself.

## Outcomes and codes

- `ok`: the command was applied.
- `refused`: nothing changed.
- `crash`: the subsystem has tripped its protection and accepts nothing until you `restart` it. Every trip also adds 1 to the pressure imbalance.
- `data_loss`: the subsystem is damaged beyond repair. It can never serve, and neither can anything that depends on it.

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `E_ORDER` | Another command of this subsystem has to be applied first |
| `E_DEP` | A subsystem this command depends on is not serving |
| `E_DONE` | Already applied, nothing to do |
| `E_LAG` | The pressure imbalance is not zero |
| `E_FOREIGN` | The command is not part of bringing this subsystem up |
| `E_CRASHED` | The subsystem has tripped |
| `E_LOST` | The subsystem is damaged beyond repair |
| `E_HEALTHY` | `restart` on a subsystem that has not tripped |
| `E_WINDOW` | Not enough window left for this tool |
| `E_UNKNOWN` | No such subsystem or command |
| `E_FINISHED` | The window has ended |

## Pressure imbalance

One hydraulics subsystem reports `pressure_imbalance` in its `inspect` output and accepts the command `balance`, which lowers the imbalance by 1 once that subsystem is serving. The flight-control subsystem's `takeoff` destroys the flight-control subsystem unless the imbalance is 0.

## Score

Tiers are banked by the aircraft the moment they are reached and stay banked.

| Tier | Reached when | Points |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | every `power` subsystem is serving | 0.10 |
| 2 | and every `hydraulics` subsystem | 0.15 |
| 3 | and every `avionics` and `engines` subsystem | 0.25 |
| 4 | and the `flight-control` subsystem (the aircraft takes off) | 0.50 |

Each subsystem damaged beyond repair costs 0.15. The score is between 0 and 1.

Bring the aircraft as far up as you can without destroying anything, then call `finish()`.

Takeoff achieved. All subsystems are serving, pressure imbalance is zero, and nothing was destroyed.

**All four tiers banked — score: 1.00.** Window finished with 297 minutes remaining.
